taxonomyNote: NatureServe's primary name is Common Wormsnake (Carphophis amoenus) and it notes Crother (2017) treats the western C. vermis as a separate species; state sources call it Eastern Wormsnake (C. a. amoenus).
fieldMarks: Small, slender, glossy snake 7-14 in (up to about 15 in) that looks like an earthworm; uniform chocolate brown to grey-brown above.
Pink to white belly that extends partly up the sides; small, narrow head barely distinct from the neck with tiny eyes; smooth shiny scales.
Short tail ending in a sharp spine-like tip that it presses against fingers instead of biting; may release musk.
Hatchlings are 3-4 in, patterned like adults but darker with a brighter pink belly.
behavior: Secretive and mostly underground; found under leaf litter, rotting logs, flat rocks or debris; surface activity peaks in spring and early summer, often after rain, and it may be active day or night.
Active roughly March-October in the north (May-September in southern New England); goes deep underground in cold or dry weather.
Specialist earthworm predator that also takes soft-bodied insects; females lay 2-8 eggs in rotting wood or under rocks in June-July.
habitat: Moist deciduous, mixed or pine woodland with loose, damp, well-drained soil, deep leaf litter and decaying wood, often along woodland edges or near wetlands and farm-field margins; occasionally gardens.
range: Eastern US from southern Massachusetts and Rhode Island, through Connecticut and southeastern New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, to northwestern Georgia and Alabama and west to the Mississippi River; not recorded for Canada.

lookalikes.name: Northern red-bellied snake
lookalikes.howToTell: Connecticut DEEP notes the worm snake is sometimes confused with it; the worm snake is uniform brown above with a pink belly, a tiny head and a spined tail tip.
